wine.name: Octagon
wine.grapes: Merlot, in most vintages the larger part, with Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot and at times Cabernet Sauvignon, in shares that change each year.
wine.sites: The estate's own vineyards around the ruins of Governor James Barbour's house at Barboursville, in the rolling hills of Orange County, within the Monticello AVA.
wine.making: Each grape is fermented apart on its skins in stainless steel for about a week, with a longer maceration after. The wine is aged for about a year in French oak barriques, part of them new; the chosen barrels are then blended and rested in steel for some months before bottling. It is made only in vintages the house judges worthy of it.
wine.glass: Blackcurrant, blueberry and plum over cedar and a leafy note of Cabernet Franc; medium in body, with fresh acidity and silky, fine tannin and a dry, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Open within a few years of release, a strong vintage gains savoury depth over a decade and more.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour ahead; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: Named for the eight sided drawing room at the heart of Jefferson's design for Governor Barbour's house.
The state of origin as the label prints it; the estate itself lies within the Monticello AVA.

records.table: Octagon is Barboursville Vineyards' Bordeaux style red from Orange County, named for the eight sided room Thomas Jefferson drew for Governor James Barbour's house, whose ruins stand on the estate. Mostly Merlot, it is made only in the years the house judges worthy.
records.story: James Barbour (1775 to 1842), governor of Virginia through the War of 1812 and later Secretary of War, built his house at Barboursville to designs supplied by his friend Thomas Jefferson (1743 to 1826); it stood complete by about 1822, with an octagonal drawing room at its heart. On Christmas Day 1884 it burned, leaving the brick walls and the columns of its porticoes, which stand as a listed landmark. The Barbour family farmed the land into the twentieth century. In 1976 the Zonin wine family of the Veneto, whose firm dates its roots to 1821, bought the estate as its one wine estate outside Italy, against local advice to plant tobacco, and set European vines where Jefferson's own at Monticello had failed. By the house's account it led the state in planting Cabernet Franc that same year. Octagon was first made with the 1991 vintage, a first attempt from young plantings, and the cellar holds that the wine found its modern shape from 1997; it is left unmade in years the house judges weak, and the 2019 was the twenty first Octagon. For a sommelier, it is the red that carries the story of Virginia wine from Jefferson onward.

others.name: Viognier Reserve
others.note: A white of the Rhône grape that Virginia named its signature in 2011.

others.name: Nebbiolo Reserve
others.note: A red of Piedmont's grape, one of the Italian varieties the Veneto founders brought to the estate.

others.name: Petit Verdot Reserve
others.note: A varietal red of a grape that also goes into Octagon; its 2010 won the Monticello Cup.

traps: Octagon is a blend of the Bordeaux grapes, not a varietal, and Barboursville's Italian grapes go into its other wines.
The house at Barboursville was designed by Jefferson for James Barbour; it is not Monticello, Jefferson's own home near Charlottesville.
Octagon is not made every year: the house leaves it unmade in vintages it judges weak.

report: Founded 1976, the ruins and the octagonal room rest on the house's Heritage page, the Virginia Department of Historic Resources and the Monticello encyclopedia; the fire of Christmas Day 1884 is in both the latter.

Octagon's first vintage 1991 rests on Wine and Country Life and Wikipedia; the modern shape from 1997 and the skipped years (2000, 2003 and 2011) come from one C-Ville interview only, so the years are not taught.
The making (steel, about a year in French barriques, part new, then months in steel) is the house's page for the 2021; the blend changes yearly, so no shares are taught.
The label's appellation is Virginia by Jancis Robinson's tasting records of the 2007 and 2010; the Monticello AVA is Wikipedia's.
The claim that the house led the state in planting Cabernet Franc in 1976 is the house's own and is hedged.
The winemaker and the founder of 1976 are living and are not named; the family is named as the house's owners of history.
The glass note draws on the house's own note (blueberry, blackcurrant, medium body, silky tannin) with the varietal make up; no independent tasting note was read.

wine.name: Viognier
wine.grapes: Viognier, the white grape of Condrieu in the northern Rhône.
wine.sites: The house's vineyards around Gordonsville in the rolling hills of Orange County, where Viognier was chosen for its thick skins and loose clusters, which resist the rot of humid Virginia summers.
wine.making: Made from Viognier grown by the house in Orange County. Its Barrel Select bottling is given time in oak, which by the house's account lifts the palate and leaves a finish of green apple. The first wines were made in a leased cellar before the house crushed in its own in 1993.
wine.glass: Honeysuckle and apricot over ripe peach and a little ginger; round and generous in texture, with modest acidity and a soft, scented finish of green apple.
wine.ageing: Made to drink young, in its first two or three years, while its perfume is fresh.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass with room for the perfume.

label.means: The grape, which Virginia named its signature grape in 2011.
The house's bottling of the grape given time in oak before release.

records.table: Horton Vineyards of Gordonsville in Orange County helped make Viognier Virginia's white: its founder chose the Rhône grape for thick skins against the humid summers, and its 1993, by the house's account, took first place at a California tasting. Pour it young and cool.
records.story: The house began in 1988, when its founder and a business partner bought land at Gordonsville in Orange County. Having studied Viognier in the Rhône and in California, he bet on it for its thick skins and loose bunches, which shrug off the rot that summer rain brings to Virginia, and he was among the first in the state to plant it. He planted Norton too, bringing the native grape of Richmond back to Virginia from Missouri, the first commercial planting of it in the state since Prohibition. The first small crop came in 1991 and was made in a leased cellar, Montdomaine; the first crush in the house's own cellar followed in 1993. That 1993 Viognier, as the house tells it, took first place at a tasting in California and turned other growers towards the grape, and in 2011 Virginia named Viognier its signature grape. The founder died in 2018. In 2019 the house's Petit Manseng of 2016 won the Governor's Cup, the first time that grape took the overall prize. For a sommelier, Horton is where the Virginia story of Viognier begins, and a house that has always grown the unusual.

others.name: Norton
others.note: The native grape of Richmond, which the house replanted commercially in Virginia; it also made a Port style wine of it.

others.name: Petit Manseng
others.note: The white grape of Jurançon; the house's 2016 won the Virginia Governor's Cup in 2019.

others.name: Rkatsiteli
others.note: A white of the Georgian grape, one of the unusual varieties the house grows.

traps: Horton replanted Norton commercially; the grape itself was raised in Richmond in the 1820s, long before the house.
Horton is at Gordonsville in Orange County, the same county as Barboursville, not in the northern hunt country around Middleburg.
The Governor's Cup of 2019 went to Horton's Petit Manseng, not to its Viognier.

questions.q: A guest asks why Viognier suits Horton's vineyards in humid Orange County. Which reason fits?

Late budding that escapes hard spring frosts
Very high acidity that needs a hot summer
Tight bunches that ripen early in drought
questions.exp: The founder chose Viognier because its thick skins and loose clusters stand up to the rot of humid summers; late budding is a guard against frost, which is not the threat named.

Petit Manseng
Rkatsiteli
Viognier
questions.exp: Norton, raised in Richmond in the 1820s, had survived in Missouri; Horton brought it back to Virginia. Petit Manseng is a French vinifera grape, not a native.

The year Viognier was first planted differs (1989 in one account, 1991 in another), so the story says only that the founder was among the first in the state to plant it; the first crop of 1991 and the first crush of 1993 rest on Wikipedia and the house.
The 1993 Viognier's first place at a California tasting rests on the house and Wikipedia only, without the competition's name, and is hedged as the house's account.

The label's appellation (Virginia) is not confirmed from a label read here, and no source gave the Viognier's vessels or élevage beyond the Barrel Select's oak, so the making says little.
The glass note draws on the house's own note (honeysuckle, green apple) with the varietal; apricot, peach and ginger are the grape's and were not read in a note of this wine.

records.place: Linden, Fauquier County, on the Blue Ridge, Virginia

wine.name: Hardscrabble Chardonnay
wine.grapes: Chardonnay alone, drawn from the Hardscrabble vineyard with vines planted in 1985 and later; some vintages blend in fruit from the house's other sites.
wine.sites: Hardscrabble, the estate vineyard around the winery on top of the Blue Ridge at about 1,350 feet, on south and east facing slopes of deep, well drained soils of granite and greenstone.
wine.making: Fermented and aged in French oak barrels from small Burgundian coopers, only a small share of them new; in later vintages fermentation starts in tank before the wine is racked to barrel. It rests on its lees for about ten months, with little stirring, and the malolactic is allowed or held back as the year asks.
wine.glass: Lemon, green apple and pear over hazelnut and a stony, saline edge; taut rather than broad, with high acidity, a light touch of oak and a long, firm finish.
wine.ageing: Tight when young, it opens after three to five years and keeps for a decade in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 11 to 13 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle briefly if it seems closed; a Burgundy glass.

label.means: The estate vineyard around the winery, named for the hard, poor farm it was made from.
The state of origin; the vineyard lies high on the Blue Ridge in Fauquier County.

records.table: Hardscrabble Chardonnay is Linden Vineyards' white from its home vineyard high on the Blue Ridge in Fauquier County: fermented in barrel, aged on its lees and kept taut by altitude. Pour it a little cool, in a Burgundy glass.
records.story: Linden began in 1983, when its founder took on an abandoned farm on the Blue Ridge near the hamlet of Linden, ground so hard to work that it gave the vineyard its name, Hardscrabble. The first vines went in in 1985, among them Chardonnay that goes into the wine, and the winery was finished in time for the harvest of 1987, the first commercial vintage. Over the following decades the house became known for wines of single vineyards, adding Avenius, a cool ridge a mile to the north planted in 1996, and Boisseau, a warmer bluff at Front Royal above the Shenandoah Valley. The house's notes show its Chardonnay changing with it: fermented wholly in barrel in the late 1990s, with the malolactic allowed in one year and stopped in the next, and from about 2012 started in tank and moved to barrel, with little new oak and less stirring, for freshness. Hardscrabble Red, a Bordeaux style blend that the 2021 vintage turned towards Cabernet Sauvignon, grows on the same slopes. For a sommelier, Linden is the Virginia house to cite on altitude and single vineyards, and its Hardscrabble Chardonnay the white that shows both.

others.name: Hardscrabble Red
others.note: The estate's Bordeaux style red from the same vineyard, led by Cabernet Sauvignon from the 2021 vintage by the house's notes.

others.name: Boisseau Red
others.note: A red from a warmer, west facing bluff at Front Royal above the Shenandoah Valley, fruit forward in style.

Linden is in Fauquier County high on the Blue Ridge, not in Loudoun County around Middleburg.

records.place: Delaplane, Fauquier County, Middleburg Virginia AVA

wine.name: Lost Mountain
wine.grapes: A Bordeaux style blend: Cabernet Sauvignon leads in most vintages, with Merlot, Cabernet Franc and Petit Verdot in shares that change, and in some years Cabernet Franc leads.
wine.sites: The estate's own knoll at Delaplane, between the Blue Ridge and Bull Run, divided into eleven parcels on steep slopes of thin clay and gravel over deep decomposed granite that drains the summer rain away.
wine.making: The blend is settled anew each year from the knoll's parcels, with a Bordeaux consultant who has worked beside the cellar since the first vintage, 2008. The wine is aged in French oak barrels, a large share of them new, before bottling at the estate.
wine.glass: Cassis, blackberry and graphite over cedar, violet and a cool, stony edge; firm and fine grained in tannin, with fresh acidity and a long, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Firm when young, it needs five to eight years, and a strong vintage keeps well beyond a decade.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The low range the vineyard's knoll stands on, between the Blue Ridge and Bull Run.
The founder's initials, which named the house and stay on its logo.

records.table: Lost Mountain is the grand red of RdV Vineyards at Delaplane: a Bordeaux style blend, Cabernet Sauvignon led in most years, from a granite knoll in the Blue Ridge foothills, made with a Bordeaux consultant since 2008. Decant it young.
records.story: The house is named by its founder's initials, RdV. A former Marine who had worked in technology, he went looking in the northern Virginia foothills for ground that would drain, and found it in a rocky knoll at Delaplane, land once judged unfit for farming, where thin clay and gravel lie over deep decomposed granite. He planted it in 2006, and from the first vintage, 2008, a Bordeaux consultant worked beside the cellar on two red blends only: Rendezvous, led by Merlot, and Lost Mountain, the grand wine, named for the low range the knoll stands on between the Blue Ridge and Bull Run. In June 2024 the estate was sold to the family behind Château Montrose, the second growth of Saint-Estèphe, and the founder stepped back. The new owners announced that the estate would take the name of its grand wine and become Lost Mountain Vineyards, keeping the old logo. For a sommelier, Lost Mountain is a Virginia red to set beside Bordeaux in a blind flight, from a house that has made two wines and nothing else.

Rendezvous, led by Merlot, is the house's other red, not its grand wine.

report: The pick stands, but the estate is renamed: after the sale of June 2024 it announced it would become Lost Mountain Vineyards, and its own site now carries that name; the integrator may wish the producer shown as Lost Mountain Vineyards (formerly RdV Vineyards) in plan.json.

Lost Mountain is the grand wine and Rendezvous the Merlot led other by Michelin and the house's pages; the claim in one source that Lost Mountain is always at least seventy per cent Cabernet Sauvignon is contradicted by the house's own page for the 2021 (Cabernet Franc led), so the grapes are hedged.
Planting in 2006 and the first vintage 2008 rest on two secondary sources; the granite soils on one visitor's account and a second profile; the knoll's eleven parcels on Wine Industry Advisor only.

The founder, the consultant, the buyers (the two brothers are in people.json) and the winemakers are living and are not named; Jane Anson's report was not cited because a writer's own site is no source.
The appellation Middleburg Virginia is the house's own page for the 2013; it was not confirmed on a label of every vintage.
The barrel time in months was not found in any source read, so the making gives none; the glass and ageing notes are general to the style and were not read in a tasting note.

wine.name: Locksley Reserve Norton
wine.grapes: Norton, the great majority, with Tannat and a little Petit Verdot in the vintages from 2017 to 2021; the blend changes with the year.
wine.sites: The Locksley Estate near Middleburg in Loudoun County, where Norton was the largest planting in the first year, 1998, and leads the vineyard.
wine.making: Made from Norton grown on the house's own estate, the blend settled anew each vintage. Norton's own deep colour and bright acidity carry the wine; Tannat adds tannin and Petit Verdot depth, in parts that have shifted over the years, with Nebbiolo in at least one vintage.
wine.glass: Dried cherry, blackberry and plum with tobacco and dried herbs; deep purple in colour, bright and juicy in acidity rather than tannic, with a firm, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Approachable on release, it keeps for a decade, its acidity holding it as the fruit dries.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant for an hour; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The native American grape raised in Richmond in the 1820s, once sold as Norton's Virginia Seedling.
Named for the Locksley Estate, the house's farm near Middleburg; the house's reserve red.

records.table: Locksley Reserve is Chrysalis Vineyards' Norton from the Locksley Estate near Middleburg: Virginia's own grape, raised in Richmond in the 1820s, deep in colour and bright in acidity, with a little Tannat for grip. Its 2021 took the first Governor's Cup gold for a Norton.
records.story: Norton is the grape a Richmond physician, Daniel Norborne Norton, who died in 1842, raised from seedlings around 1820; a nurseryman's catalogue listed it in 1822 as Norton's Virginia Seedling. It thrived where European vines failed, travelled west, and in 1873 a Norton from Hermann, Missouri, took a gold medal at the Vienna World's Fair. Missouri kept the grape alive, and it came back to Virginia only in 1989. Chrysalis was founded to champion it: its founder planted the first vines at the Locksley Estate near Middleburg in 1998, and Norton was the largest planting of that first year. The house holds that it grows the largest single planting of Norton anywhere, a claim of its own, beside Albariño, Viognier and other European grapes. In 2009 the farm became the Chrysalis Vineyards and Locksley Estate Agricultural and Forestal District, which protects its fields. Locksley Reserve, its Norton led red, made history in 2024, when its 2021 vintage became the first Norton to win a gold medal at the Virginia Governor's Cup. For a sommelier, it is the bottle that answers what Virginia's own grape tastes like.

others.name: Estate Bottled Norton
others.note: The house's straight Norton from the estate, beside the reserve.

others.name: Albariño
others.note: The Galician white grape, grown on the estate and made in homage to the wines of Spain.

traps: The Norton that won gold at Vienna in 1873 was a Missouri wine from Hermann, not a Virginian one.
Norton is a native American grape, not one of Europe's vinifera, though Locksley Reserve blends a little Tannat into it.
Chrysalis is at Middleburg in Loudoun County, not at Gordonsville, where Horton brought Norton back to Virginia.
